nm_shield.blurb: A huge face on the north side of Juan Tabo Canyon, high on the west flank of the Sandia Mountains above Albuquerque. This is mostly long traditional climbing, with some lines stacking up to around eleven pitches, plus a lone aid line, a winter snow route and one easy-fifth-class scramble up a ridge. Difficulty runs from the 5.5 and 5.6 range up to hard 5.12 and a 5.13, though most lines sit between 5.6 and 5.11. Rock quality changes from pitch to pitch and the crux sections can be bold, so it suits experienced parties. Expect a long day, plenty of solitude and no water on the wall.

nm_capulet_side_canyon.blurb: A small side drainage off Capulin Canyon in the Jemez Mountains, holding around twenty traditional crack lines. Every route is under 100 feet. Most climbs fall in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with a few easier 5.9s and a handful of 5.12s, so it suits climbers who are comfortable leading cracks in the 5.10s. The rock is volcanic tuff that takes gear well but can be loose and dirty, so bring a helmet and test holds. The side canyon holds more shade than the main canyon and sees fewer visitors than the main walls, which makes for a quiet day. Reaching it involves a steep, rugged hike down into the canyon system.

nm_northwest_passage_the.blurb: A friendly cluster of short volcanic-rock routes on the east side of Luna Park, in the Red Rock Arroyo zone northeast of Monticello, in the desert hills of southern New Mexico. Twenty climbs mix bolted sport lines (the majority) with traditional routes and one top-rope. Grades stay approachable, running from 5.6 to 5.10, with the bulk in the 5.9 and 5.10 range, so it works well for newer leaders and mixed groups. The cliff sits in a stand of trees, and you get to it through a gap in the lowest band of rock; and a forest campground is close by. The pass-top setting can get very windy when weather fronts move through.
